description: Drama Years 3-4 width tiers — ACARA v9. All strands are capability strands; primary axis is task_contexts.
subject: Drama

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the command term. For Y3-4, minimum is the command term met in one task context — one improvised piece, one performance, one drama example observed with analysis.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope from elaborations — the range of contexts a well-taught Y3-4 class would engage with. Includes a range of dramatic forms and analytical contexts.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment adding new task types, cultural or historical contexts, or perspectives — not harder versions of the same activity.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are the primary source. First Nations elaborations for E02 appear in wider; other standards include First Nations directions where elaborations indicate them.

AC9ADR4C01.minimum_width: Student contributes to devising a drama with at least one other person that communicates a recognisable idea or perspective through at least two deliberate element choices.
AC9ADR4C01.typical_width: Students improvise and devise drama exploring roles and situations they initiate; they use elements and story principles (time, place, role, character) to shape improvisations; they work collaboratively to devise drama using process drama strategies and play-building; they communicate Acknowledgement of Country before performances where appropriate.
wider: Students improvise drama exploring situations from another time or place, using empathy to imagine themselves as participants in historical or cross-cultural events
Students devise dialogue for a 'wordless story' or create dramatic action for a story known only through audio sources
Students devise drama communicating their connection to a place in their community, drawing on First Nations Australians' drama about Country/Place as a starting point
Students devise a 'miniature world' drama with a complex fictional space, consistent rules and multiple character relationships
elaborations: using learning from First Nations Australians' drama to devise drama communicating connection to place
creating drama by exploring roles and situations in a 'miniature world'
improvising drama to explore issues, using empathy to take on roles and 'stand in the shoes' of another
devising dialogue for a previously 'wordless story'
using elements of drama and principles of story to shape improvisations
working in groups to devise sections of drama and combining them using play-building
communicating Acknowledgement of Country before a performance

AC9ADR4D01.minimum_width: Student makes at least two deliberate element choices — one vocal and one spatial/movement — in an improvised or devised sequence, and can name and explain each.
AC9ADR4D01.typical_width: Students experiment with voice (loudness, pace, pitch) to create roles, situations and atmosphere; they develop spatial awareness using proximity and movement to manipulate tension; they explore language choice and tone; they practise connecting scenes through rhythmic or movement transitions.
wider: Students compare how the same dialogue produces different dramatic effects with different vocal delivery
Students investigate how stillness and silence function as dramatic tools — not just as pauses — in building tension and focus
Students explore how status and power relationships between characters can be communicated entirely through spatial choices (proximity, levels, orientation)
elaborations: experimenting with loudness/softness, pace and pitch of voices to create roles and situations
exploring roles using language choice, expressions and tone to heighten tension
improvising ways to connect short scenes through clapping, phrases or movement
developing spatial awareness — considering distance and movement to manipulate tension

AC9ADR4E01.minimum_width: Student identifies a purpose for a drama from a given cultural or historical context and names at least one feature or idea they could apply in their own drama-making.
AC9ADR4E01.typical_width: Students listen to actors discuss character development; they reflect on live and recorded performances asking questions about purpose and cultural context; they compare audience and performer expectations in different cultural settings; they examine drama in their community and compare it with drama from other cultures, times and places.
wider: Students investigate puppetry or physical theatre from another culture or historical period, comparing it with examples from their community
Students investigate drama from a country or region in Asia, exploring its conventions, purposes and audience relationships
Students research a specific historical drama tradition and analyse how its conventions reflect the social context in which it developed
elaborations: listening to actors talk about how they developed their character and what they found interesting
comparing audience and performer expectations in different cultural settings including Asia
reflecting on live or recorded performances asking questions about purpose and features
examining drama in their community and comparing it with drama from other cultures, times and places

AC9ADR4E02.minimum_width: Student describes at least one way First Nations drama communicates connection to or responsibility for Country/Place, and identifies one element of drama used to do this.
AC9ADR4E02.typical_width: Students collect and share information about First Nations drama for festivals, ceremonies and cultural occasions; they explore how First Nations Australians use drama to maintain cultural knowledge and unique ways of life; they observe how elements (place, language, movement) communicate connection to Country/Place in drama they access using co-created resources.
wider: Students access First Nations drama communicating ways to live sustainably and care for land, sea, sky or waterways
Students explore performances representing the importance of Country/Place and Story as a starting point for discussing different ways of seeing the same place
Students compare how First Nations drama from different communities represents connection to Country/Place, noting both shared themes and distinctive cultural expressions
elaborations: collecting and sharing information about First Nations drama for festivals or ceremonies communicating knowledge about Country/Place
exploring how First Nations Australians use drama to communicate knowledge and maintain unique ways of life
observing how elements of drama are used in First Nations drama to communicate connection to Country/Place
accessing drama by First Nations Australians exploring ways to live sustainably and respect the land
looking at performances representing the importance of Country/Place and Story as a starting point for talking about different ways of seeing the same place

AC9ADR4P01.minimum_width: Student performs improvised or devised drama in an informal setting, remaining in role and making at least two performance choices (vocal and physical) that contribute to dramatic meaning.
AC9ADR4P01.typical_width: Students perform in informal settings demonstrating commitment to role; they use voice, movement and language to sustain role and relationships; they manipulate focus, tension, space and time in the performance; they vary facial expressions and movements to create roles and situations.
wider: Students perform a drama based on a story from another time or culture, adapting performance choices to suit the context
Students perform in multiple informal contexts (class, another class, small community audience), adapting to different audience sizes and familiarity
Students evaluate their performance using structured reflection — comparing what they intended with what the audience experienced
elaborations: using voice, movement and language to sustain role and relationships when performing
demonstrating commitment to the reality of the drama — staying in role throughout
manipulating focus, tension, space and time to shape dramatic action when performing
